# AI gives everyone the average. Four places where judgment matters

I gave ChatGPT, Claude and Figma Make the same brief, once for a music app and once for a bank app. Each time, all three handed back what was essentially the same app.

None of them knew anything about the brand, the users or the code that already existed. These tools learned from everything ever published, so when we bring nothing, they return the most common answer: the average. Everyone who asks gets the same one back.

Compare that with Spotify, Apple Music and SoundCloud, or Revolut, Monzo and Nubank. Same categories, and yet each is a different product with its own identity and its own customers. The tools can't give us that difference if we bring nothing.

## Four places, in the order of the work

I see four places where we are losing human judgment, in the order the work happens. Together they spell KEEP, because this is how we keep what is ours.

→ Know, before you open the tool
→ Encode, when you set it up
→ Explore, while you work
→ Polish, before you deliver

![KEEP: Know, Encode, Explore, Polish, the four places where human judgment still matters, in the order of the work](images/t1-li-1.png)
*KEEP follows the order of the work.*

Each one is a trade-off. Below, for each: what we gain, what we risk, a real example and what to do.

## Know, before you open the tool

→ What we gain: hours back, and no more blank page.
→ What we risk: solving, very fast, a problem that was never the client's problem, with the same answer as everyone else.

A friend of mine is an osteopath. He knew nothing about programming, and no product solved his problem; nothing even connected to the device he uses with his patients. He built something small with AI, showed it to me, and I told him to keep going. It now covers patients, appointments and prescriptions, connects to his device, runs on desktop and mobile, and already has two clients. He didn't write one line of code. What he had was years of living the problem every day.

What to do: the tool knows everything that was published, but not who you are building for or how the industry works from the inside. That isn't on the internet. It's in people. Go and get it before you open the tool: talk to the people who use it, understand the business, ask questions.

It's uncomfortable for those of us who build for a living, me included: **someone who really knows a business can now build a good product more easily than someone who only builds what they're asked to.**

## Encode, when you set it up

→ What we gain: a decent result on the first try.
→ What we risk: it isn't our brand, it doesn't serve our users, and it doesn't fit what already exists.

Before, there was always someone in the room who knew the rules by heart; now things get built without that person nearby. Most AI tools reach for shadcn by default, a very good free component library. Give the machine nothing of your own, and that is the system you get, the same as everyone else's.

On one project, creating a new component took weeks: requirements, exploring solutions, testing, development and QA, with the information spread everywhere. We built a design system accelerator that puts all of that context in one place the machine can read. For the same scope, the same process went from weeks to hours.

![How the accelerator works: you connect your tools once, it proposes three options and you pick one, it builds and tests while you review what it flags, and nothing is merged until an engineer approves](images/t1-li-2.png)
*AI accelerates. People decide.*

It's fast because the machine has the context, and it's done well because there is always a name next to the decision. The accelerator reads the ticket, asks questions and proposes three options; you pick one. It writes the code and runs the checks; you review what it flags. Nothing is merged until an engineer approves.

What to do: write down what already exists (the brand, the design system, the code) and the decisions already made, in a place the machine can read. If it isn't written there, for the machine it doesn't exist.

## Explore, while you work

→ What we gain: we deliver fast, and nobody complains.
→ What we risk: we stop at the first idea, and the client stops needing us.

This is the one that worries me most in a company like ours. We ran a short design sprint with people from a client's business, none of them designers, and none of whom had used a design tool before. In one afternoon, they built working prototypes. If our job is only to do what we're asked, they can already do it without us.

The same sprint showed what we add. Everyone worked on the same real problem from their own business, and each group had a facilitator, one of our designers or product people, as a guide rather than a creator. Every group came back with a different solution, each one based on a different user context. Then the teams swapped and tested each other's prototypes, AI organised the improvements, and people chose what went in. With one team only, we would have stopped at the first idea.

What to do: if AI makes one version cheap, it also makes ten cheap. Go past the first idea, look for alternatives, and get other people to critique the work instead of relying on intuition alone.

## Polish, before you deliver

→ What we gain: less review, and fewer meetings.
→ What we risk: the mistake looks good, so it gets through.

This is the hardest of the four, because the first result fools you. We were hiring, and every candidate's personal website had the same layout, the same gradient and the same sentences. I couldn't tell if I was evaluating the candidate or Claude. They did nothing wrong; they all did the same thing.

For a marketing video for one of our accelerators, I didn't want the first characters the tool gave me, because most AI videos look alike now. So I ran a casting in Higgsfield: seventy-one candidates until I had the cast I wanted. One boat scene went through twenty-two versions, and I kept two. AI saved me no work there. It gave me more attempts, until the scene was right.

What to do: the bar doesn't go down because something was made with AI. AI gives you the first version, and the good version is your decision. You don't have to polish everything, only the places where people feel it.

## A checklist for your next piece of work

Before you open the tool
→ I have spoken with people who live the problem.
→ I can explain how the business works from the inside.

When you set it up
→ Our brand, design system and code are written where the machine can read them.
→ The decisions already made are written down, with a name next to each.

While you work
→ I went past the first idea and compared real alternatives.
→ Someone other than me critiqued it before I chose.

Before you deliver
→ I have reviewed the parts people will feel.
→ The bar didn't go down because it was made with AI.

![The KEEP checklist: eight checks across Know, Encode, Explore and Polish](images/t1-li-3.png)
*Two checks for each part of KEEP.*

## If you lead a team

Don't just tell a team to use AI. If all the time AI saves goes into delivering more of the same, we just get more things that look the same. Someone has to decide that part of that time goes back into the product.

**Give part of the time AI saves back to quality, and protect it in the plan.** Then make room to imagine other experiences, not only faster screens.

Without AI, my friend would not have his app, the component would still take weeks, the sprint would not have produced working prototypes in one afternoon, and I would not have made twenty-two versions of the boat. When everyone has the same tools, the tools stop being the difference. What others can't copy is people who care more.

Which of the four does your team skip most often right now: Know, Encode, Explore or Polish?

## Promo post

Three AI tools, one brief, the same app.

I gave ChatGPT, Claude and Figma Make the same brief for a music app, then for a bank app. None of them knew the brand, the users or the code that already existed, so all three returned the most common answer.

When everyone uses the same tools and brings nothing, everyone gets the same average.

I wrote an article on the four places in the work where human judgment still makes the difference:

→ Know, before you open the tool
→ Encode, when you set it up
→ Explore, while you work
→ Polish, before you deliver

Each part has the trade we are making (what we gain, what we risk), a real example, and what to do about it. One example: a design system component that went from weeks to hours once the machine had all the context.

There is also a checklist you can use on your next piece of work, and a note for anyone who leads a team.

Which of the four does your team skip most often?
